pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budgeting via period split
situation: Two blocks (or a block and top-level interconnect) are implemented separately and communicate synchronously across a boundary; each block's SDC needs input_delay/output_delay values before the other side exists in netlist form.
derivation: Start from the shared clock period T at the boundary. Subtract an estimated interconnect delay (wire + any boundary buffering) I, estimated early from floorplan wire-load or a placeholder (e.g. 10-15% of T for a typical reasonably-sized block-to-block wire). The remaining budget (T - I) is split between the launching block's internal output path and the receiving block's internal input path, often roughly proportional to each side's logic depth expectation, but a common starting split is 50/50 when no better info exists. So output_delay on the driving block's SDC = I + (share allocated to receive side), and input_delay on the receiving block's SDC reflects the same I plus driver-side share, expressed as 'time already consumed before this pin'. Iterating: as floorplan matures, replace the wire-load estimate with actual RC-extracted or global-route-estimated delay.
wrong_way: Giving both blocks the full period T as available budget without subtracting interconnect delay (i.e., forgetting interconnect is shared, not free), or worse, having each block's owner independently assume they get most of the period, causing double-booking. This silently breaks at integration when actual interconnect delay eats into both sides' assumed slack, and violations only appear at chip-level timing, far too late to easily fix.
defense: Point to the interconnect delay estimate's source (early floorplan wire-load model or a prior similar block's actual number), show the 50/50 or logic-depth-weighted split explicitly in a spreadsheet, and cross-check that summed input_delay + output_delay assumptions from both block owners equal (T - I), not more.
signoff_risk: Too tight (budget assumed smaller interconnect delay than reality): chip-level setup violations at the boundary that require late ECOs or spec relaxation. Too loose (budget over-allocated interconnect delay, starving block-internal budget less than needed): blocks close individually with margin to spare, wasting achievable frequency, discovered only when someone asks why the chip is slower than either block's standalone number.
node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, interconnect delay is a much larger fraction of period than at 28nm, so the naive 50/50 split is less defensible and teams more often insist on an RC-based estimate even at floorplan stage
_numeric_confidence_notes: assumes interconnect estimate around 10-15% of period as a common starting point (confidence 0.4); assumes 50/50 split as a common default absent better data (confidence 0.45)

pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision for slow/quasi-static control signals
situation: A path exists in the timing graph (e.g., a mode-select, configuration register, or reset synchronizer output feeding combinational logic) but the signal is known to change far less often than every clock cycle, and normal single-cycle timing would be needlessly hard or impossible to meet.
derivation: First determine whether the path is truly never required to be sampled correctly on the very next cycle after a change (justifies false_path) versus is allowed extra cycles but must still eventually be captured correctly within N cycles (justifies multicycle_path -setup N). The distinguishing question: does functional correctness ever depend on the receiving logic seeing the new value within a bounded number of cycles? If yes, use multicycle with N derived from the known minimum interval between legal changes of the source signal (e.g., a signal architecturally guaranteed to be stable for at least 4 cycles after any change becomes 'set_multicycle_path 4 -setup' with a corresponding 'set_multicycle_path 3 -hold' to keep the hold check aligned to the cycle before the new setup edge). If the path is fundamentally asynchronous or functionally irrelevant to timing (e.g., a scan/test-only path, or a signal whose value at the sampling edge genuinely never matters), false_path is used instead.
wrong_way: Applying false_path to a signal that actually does need to be captured within a bounded time (common shortcut to 'make timing pass'), which silently removes the path from all timing analysis so a real functional timing failure (data changing too close to a legitimate sample point) is never caught by STA and only shows up as an intermittent functional bug in silicon or emulation.
defense: Cite the RTL/microarchitectural guarantee (e.g., a documented minimum hold-time-in-cycles for the control signal, enforced by a counter or handshake in the design) as the basis for the multicycle N, and show the corresponding hold multicycle adjustment (N-1) was also applied so hold checking wasn't silently left at the default single-cycle hold window, which would over-constrain hold and cause unnecessary buffer insertion.
signoff_risk: Too tight (using single-cycle timing or too small an N when the real guarantee is looser): wastes implementation effort meeting an unnecessarily hard constraint, sometimes forcing pipeline stages that aren't functionally needed. Too loose (false_path where multicycle was appropriate, or N larger than the real guarantee): real setup/hold problems on that path are masked and can cause silicon failures that STA never flagged.
_numeric_confidence_notes: the example of 'stable for at least 4 cycles -> multicycle 4/3' is illustrative only (confidence 0.3 that this specific number pattern generalizes; the setup-N/hold-N-1 relationship itself is standard and confidence is higher, ~0.6)

situation: Early in physical implementation (initial placement, early CTS), before parasitics and final library corners are accurate, teams often run timing at a tighter clock period than the actual target to build in margin against later degradation.
derivation: Take the true target period T_target and apply a margin percentage M (commonly discussed in the range of 5-10% early on, sometimes more at very early floorplan stages) to get the working period used in early optimization: T_work = T_target * (1 - M). As the design matures (post-route, signoff parasitics available, real OCV/derate applied), M is reduced stage by stage until T_work converges to T_target (or slightly above it, since some residual margin is normal even at final signoff).
wrong_way: Keeping the same large early-stage margin all the way through to signoff without relaxing it, which silently wastes area/power (cells oversized, extra buffering) chasing a target no longer necessary, or conversely relaxing the margin too early (before parasitics are trustworthy) so the design looks like it's closing timing when in fact later corners will blow through the true target once real interconnect delay is added.
defense: Show the margin-reduction schedule tied to specific implementation milestones (e.g., 'margin relaxed only after post-route parasitics extracted, not before'), and present trend data of slack at each stage to justify that the margin was earning real protection against known sources of change (OCV widening, layer assignment, clock tree insertion) rather than being an arbitrary number.
signoff_risk: Too tight (margin never relaxed): area/power penalty and possibly missed schedule chasing an artificially hard target. Too loose (margin removed too early or too small from the start): signoff timing violations appear late when the real corners and parasitics are in, often surfacing after the design was believed closed, forcing late ECOs under schedule pressure.
node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, the gap between early-stage and signoff-stage estimates is typically larger due to increased variation and multi-corner/multi-mode complexity, so margin schedules tend to be more conservative and staged more finely than at 28nm
_numeric_confidence_notes: assumes 5-10% early margin as a commonly recalled starting range (confidence 0.4)

pattern_name: Virtual clock definition for primary I/O timing
situation: A block's inputs or outputs are timed relative to an external device or another chip whose internal clock structure is not part of this block's netlist (e.g., a chip-level I/O interface), so there's no physical clock object in this block to reference for input_delay/output_delay.
derivation: Define a virtual clock (create_clock with no -add to any real pin, just a name) with the same period and, critically, the same relationship (edge alignment/phase) as the external device's clock is specified to have relative to this chip's I/O clock. input_delay and output_delay values are then set relative to this virtual clock, using the external device's specified setup/hold or valid-delay windows (from its datasheet or interface spec) translated into the input_delay/output_delay arithmetic: for an input, input_delay = external device's clock-to-out max delay + board/trace delay; for an output, output_delay = external receiving device's required setup time + board/trace delay.
wrong_way: Reusing the block's internal core clock object directly as if it were the interface clock without checking whether the actual I/O clock has different phase alignment or period (e.g., due to PLL phase shift or a different divide ratio), which silently mis-times every I/O path relative to the real external timing relationship and is often only caught in board bring-up, not simulation or STA.
defense: Reference the interface specification document's timing diagram directly (datasheet setup/hold or valid-delay numbers) as the source of the input_delay/output_delay arithmetic, and show that the virtual clock's period/edges match the documented external clock relationship, not an assumption.
signoff_risk: Too tight (input_delay/output_delay assumed worse external timing than actual): wastes internal timing budget, potentially forcing unnecessary pipeline stages on I/O paths. Too loose (assumed better external timing than actual, e.g., ignoring board trace delay): real interface timing failures only appear at board bring-up since STA showed the path passing.
_numeric_confidence_notes: no specific numbers asserted beyond the general arithmetic shape

situation: A clock is produced inside the design by dividing or gating a root clock (e.g., a simple toggle flip-flop divider or clock-gating cell producing a slower derived clock domain) and STA needs a correct create_generated_clock rather than an independent create_clock that could desynchronize from the source.
derivation: Use create_generated_clock referencing the source clock pin and the actual divide/multiply relationship implemented in the divider logic (e.g., -divide_by 2 for a simple toggle divider), applied at the output pin of the generating register/cell, so the tool derives the generated clock's period, waveform, and phase alignment automatically from the source clock rather than being independently specified. Verify the generated clock's edges align with the expected functional behavior of the divider (e.g., confirming which edge of the source clock the divided clock toggles on) by checking the divider's actual logic, not assuming a textbook 50% duty cycle divider.
wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as an independent create_clock with a manually computed period, which loses the phase/edge relationship to the source clock entirely; this silently makes the tool treat the two clock domains as unrelated (effectively asynchronous) for timing purposes, so crossing paths between the root clock and the derived clock get analyzed with incorrect (often overly pessimistic or, if false-pathed, dangerously optimistic) skew assumptions instead of the true, tool-derivable relationship.
defense: Show the divider RTL/schematic and confirm the create_generated_clock's -divide_by (or -multiply_by) and -edges settings match the actual logic implementation, and demonstrate in the generated clock's reported waveform (from the tool) that it matches the expected functional divided waveform.
signoff_risk: Too tight/wrong relationship (e.g., wrong edge assumed): paths between root and divided domain may show false violations that get incorrectly 'fixed' by adding unnecessary margin or exceptions, or conversely real violations get masked because the tool thinks the domains are unrelated. Too loose (treating as fully asynchronous when it's not): crossing paths lose the benefit of the known, analyzable relationship and either get over-margined (wasting timing) or under-constrained if someone false-paths them assuming asynchrony that doesn't actually exist.

pattern_name: Asynchronous clock-domain-crossing (CDC) constraint via false_path plus synchronizer awareness
situation: A signal crosses from one clock domain to a genuinely unrelated (asynchronous) clock domain through a synchronizer (e.g., a 2-flop synchronizer chain), and the path between the two domains needs an SDC exception since no valid static timing relationship exists between the clocks.
derivation: Apply set_false_path (or set_clock_groups -asynchronous for the whole domain pair, if broader) specifically from the synchronizer's first-stage input to its capturing flop, so STA does not attempt to compute a meaningless setup/hold check across unrelated clocks. Critically, the false_path (or async group) is scoped as narrowly as possible -- typically just the crossing point itself -- so that all other timing within each domain (including from the synchronizer's output onward) remains fully and normally checked; the exception must not accidentally blanket-cover logic that is not actually part of the crossing.
wrong_way: Applying a broad set_clock_groups -asynchronous between the two entire clock domains (rather than scoping to just the crossing flops) when there are actually other legitimate, related paths between those domains elsewhere in the design (e.g., a shared reset tree or a second, intentionally synchronous path), which silently removes real timing checks on paths that do need them, masking genuine violations elsewhere in the two domains' interaction.
defense: Point to the synchronizer's schematic/RTL showing it is a proper multi-flop synchronizer (not a single flop, which would be a metastability/CDC design bug independent of SDC), and show the false_path/async-group scoping is limited to exactly the crossing pins, verified by checking the SDC exception report for unintended path coverage.
signoff_risk: Too broad an exception (covers more than the true crossing): real synchronous paths elsewhere between the domains lose timing coverage, and violations there go undetected until functional failure. Missing or too narrow an exception (crossing not excepted at all): STA reports a spurious, unfixable 'violation' on an inherently asynchronous path, which teams sometimes 'fix' by adding meaningless buffering that does nothing for actual metastability risk (which is a separate CDC/MTBF concern, not a static timing one).

pattern_name: Interconnect budgeting between two not-yet-implemented blocks using a placeholder wire-load/RC estimate
situation: At RTL/early floorplan stage, two blocks that will eventually be connected through top-level routing need boundary timing constraints (input_delay/output_delay) before either block or the top-level interconnect has real layout.
derivation: Estimate interconnect delay using a rough distance-based or wire-load-model-based number derived from the expected floorplan (e.g., block A and B are expected to be roughly adjacent vs across the die), producing a placeholder delay value I_est. This I_est is subtracted from the shared period the same way as boundary budgeting (see the period-split pattern), but flagged explicitly as provisional pending floorplan. A tracking mechanism (e.g., a budget spreadsheet or comment in the SDC) records the assumption so it can be revisited once floorplan or global-route estimates are available.
wrong_way: Treating the early placeholder I_est as final and never revisiting it once real floorplan/placement data exists, so if the actual distance between the blocks turns out much larger than assumed (e.g., a late floorplan change moves one block across the die), the boundary timing silently becomes wrong and isn't caught until block-level or chip-level signoff, by which point both blocks may have already been 'closed' to the wrong budget.
defense: Show the placeholder estimate is explicitly labeled provisional and tied to a specific floorplan assumption (e.g., 'assumes blocks share an edge'), with a defined checkpoint (e.g., 'to be revisited at floorplan freeze') rather than presented as a firm number.
signoff_risk: Too tight (I_est assumed larger than reality): blocks over-budget for interconnect, individually closing with unnecessary margin, wasted effort. Too loose (I_est assumed smaller than the eventual real distance): chip-level integration reveals a boundary timing violation that neither block owner expected, often discovered late and expensive to fix since both blocks were independently signed off against the wrong assumption.
node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, placeholder interconnect estimates are far riskier because wire delay is proportionally larger and less linear with distance, so teams more often insist on at least a rough global-route-based estimate rather than a pure wire-load-model guess even at early stages
_numeric_confidence_notes: no specific numeric margin asserted; pattern is about process/tracking discipline rather than a specific arithmetic constant
